content: 1. The CDC, along with its planners and content experts, has disclosed that they have no financial interests or relationships with manufacturers of commercial products, suppliers of commercial services, or commercial supporters. 2. Presentations will not include any discussion of the off-label use of a product or investigational use of a product. 3. The National Association of State Public Health Veterinarians (NASPHV) recognizes the positive benefits of human-animal interaction. 4. While it is impossible to eliminate all risks associated with animal contact, this report provides recommendations to minimize the risk of disease and injury. 5. NASPHV recommends that local and state public health, agricultural, environmental, and wildlife agencies use these recommendations to establish their own guidelines or regulations to reduce the risk of disease transmission from human-animal contact in public settings. 6. Public venues where animal contact is permitted include animal displays, petting zoos, animal swap meets, pet stores, zoological institutions, nature parks, circuses, carnivals, farm tours, livestock-birthing exhibits, county or state fairs, schools, and wildlife photo opportunities. 7. Managers of these venues should use the information in this report to reduce the risk of disease transmission. 8. Guidelines have been developed to reduce risks of disease transmission from animals in healthcare and veterinary facilities, as well as from service animals (e.g., guide dogs). However, these settings are not specifically addressed in this report, though the general principles and recommendations are applicable. 9. Contact with animals in public settings, such as fairs, farm tours, petting zoos, and schools, provides opportunities for entertainment and education. 10. Zoonotic diseases, or zoonoses, are diseases transmitted from animals to humans. Of particular concern are instances where large numbers of people become ill. 11. Since 1991, approximately 50 human infectious disease outbreaks involving animals in public settings have been reported to the CDC. 12. Over the past decade, there has been an increasing number of enteric disease outbreaks associated with animals in public settings, such as fairs and petting zoos. 13. Reported outbreaks, diseases, or injuries attributed to human-animal interactions in public settings have been documented, and comments or suggestions from NASPHV members and public inquiries have been solicited. 14. In November 2006, NASPHV members and external expert consultants convened at the CDC in Atlanta, Georgia, to review scientific information on recent outbreaks, associated risk factors, pathogen biology, and interventional studies. 15. A moderated discussion of each section of the recommendations was conducted, and the committee reviewed scientific evidence and expert opinions to revise the document. A consensus was required to add or modify existing language or recommendations. 16. Enteric (intestinal) infections caused by bacteria and parasites pose the highest risk for human disease from animals in public settings. Healthy animals can harbor human enteric pathogens, many of which have a low infectious dose. 17. Due to the popularity of animal venues, a substantial number of people may be exposed. Illness and outbreaks of enteric diseases among visitors to fairs, farms, and petting zoos are well-documented. 18. Pathogens responsible for outbreaks include Escherichia coli O157:H7 and other Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), Campylobacter, Salmonella, and Cryptosporidium. 19. Although cattle, sheep, and goats are often identified as sources of infection, poultry, rodents, and other domestic and wild animals are also potential sources. 20. The primary mode of transmission for enteric pathogens is fecal-oral. Animal fur, hair, skin, and saliva can become contaminated with fecal organisms, leading to transmission when individuals pet, touch, feed, or are licked by animals. 21. Transmission has also occurred from fecal contamination of food, including raw milk, sticky foods (e.g., cotton candy), and water. Illness has been associated with contaminated clothing, shoes, animal bedding, flooring, barriers, and other environmental surfaces. 22. Animals carrying enteric pathogens pathogenic to humans, such as STEC, Salmonella, and Campylobacter, often exhibit no signs of illness and can shed these pathogens intermittently. 23. Removing ill animals, especially those with diarrhea, is necessary but not sufficient to protect animal and human health. Healthy-appearing animals often shed pathogens that contaminate the environment. 24. Some pathogens can survive for months or years in the environment. Intermittent shedding and limitations of laboratory tests mean that culturing fecal specimens or attempting to identify, screen, and remove infected animals might reduce but will not eliminate the risk of transmission. 25. Antimicrobial treatment of animals cannot reliably eliminate infection and shedding of enteric pathogens or prevent reinfection. 26. Multiple factors increase the probability of disease transmission at animal exhibits. Stress from prolonged transportation, confinement, crowding, and increased handling by people can increase pathogen shedding in animals. 27. Commingling of animals increases the likelihood that animals shedding organisms will infect other animals. 28. The prevalence of certain enteric pathogens is often higher in young animals, which are frequently used in petting zoos and educational programs. 29. Shedding of STEC and Salmonella is highest in the summer and fall when many traveling animal exhibits, agricultural fairs, and petting zoos are scheduled. 30. The risk of infections is increased by certain human factors and behaviors, especially in children. These factors include lack of awareness of disease risks, inadequate handwashing, lack of close supervision, and hand-to-mouth activities (e.g., use of pacifiers, thumb-sucking, and eating). 31. Children are particularly attracted to animal venues and have an increased risk of serious infections. 32. The layout and maintenance of facilities and animal exhibits can also affect the risk of infection. Risk factors include inadequate handwashing facilities, structural deficiencies in temporary food-service facilities, inappropriate visitor flow, and incomplete separation between animal exhibits and food preparation and consumption areas. 33. Contaminated or inadequately maintained drinking water and sewage or manure disposal systems also pose risks. 34. Lessons from outbreaks demonstrate the importance of proper facility design, maintenance, and implementation of disease-prevention recommendations.
